full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** The first pass was right. What the simulation shows is a lattice that collapses almost completely into one type, with defectors as the likely winner. That is a trivial, nearly absorbing outcome, not a new emergent pattern.

**Rule 1 on its own is a textbook model.** It is the Nowak–May spatial Prisoner's Dilemma: every agent plays the game with all his neighbors (once with each neighbor) and with himself (Moore neighborhood), then adopts the strategy of one of the agents in this set who has obtained the greatest payoff. Nowak and May used R=1.0, T=b (1.0 < b < 2.0) and S=P=0.0. Your S=−0.5 is a stricter dilemma. Later work studied the case when S=-0.01, -0.1 and S=-0.5 with this same imitate-the-best rule. On small lattices, the documented result for imitate-the-best is that the asymptotic level of cooperation is either 0 or a large value close to 1, depending on the initial condition. Your rule-1-only run (largest domain 0.991) matches that kind of near-total takeover.

**Rule 2 is a known kind of extension.** Making cooperators defect with some probability is the Mukherji et al. (1996) extension, where after following the Nowak and May update rule, each cooperator has a small independent chance of defecting. In those studies, the density of cooperators quickly decreases with p. Your version only fires when a cooperator has at least 4 defector neighbours, but it still only ever turns cooperators into defectors. So it just strengthens a drift toward all-defection that is already documented.

**Why the features look trivial or artifactual:**
- **Largest domain 0.966, about 2 domains:** n_domains appears to be log(1+n), since 1.0986 = ln 3. So one type covers roughly 97% of the lattice, with perhaps one leftover patch.
- **Correlation length 6.5:** this mostly measures how uniform the lattice is. It doesn't show a structured pattern.
- **Activity CV 0.8 and 1 reversal:** these fit a single transient followed by occasional stochastic flips. That is not the ongoing churn of Nowak–May "spatial chaos".
- **The knock-out comparison proves little:** both rules read neighbours, so removing interaction leaves a frozen random field. Any coarsening process would beat that baseline. Rule 2 alone fills the whole lattice with one type (largest domain 1.0), and rule 1 alone gets to 0.991, so the near-uniform state needs no special explanation. Strictly, the full program differs from both sub-programs, but only by a small leftover patch of cooperators plus a few stochastic flips.

**Limits:** I ran one search and didn't find a paper with exactly this neighbour-threshold defection rule. The verdict rests on the behaviour (near-total takeover by one type) being documented, not on the exact rule set.
